# Draft:Battle of Lučenec

The Battle of Lučenec (7 September 1451) was a battle between the army led by John Jiskra of Brandýs and the Hungarian army of John Hunyadi. Jiskra's army, which included a detachment of former Czech and Slovak brothers with the participation of John Talafús and others, defeated the much larger army of the Hungarian leader.
The battle, in terms of scope and number of combatants, is one of the largest armed clashes in medieval Slovak history. It was also the only defeat of Ján Huňady, in which a numerically much weaker army forced him to retreat. This alone testifies to Jiskra’s leadership talent. Hungarian chroniclers favorable to Huňady, who were later materially supported mainly by King Matthias Corvinus (son of Ján Huňady), tried to justify the defeat mainly by treachery within his army (allegedly due to betrayal by István Pelsőczi).
Build-up to the Battle
After the death of Albrecht Habsburg (1439), part of the west-oriented Hungarian estates recognized his son Ladislaus (Ladislaus Posthumous was barely 5 years old and unable to rule), opposing, mainly on the eastern side of the divide, the Polish king Vladislav II Jagiełło from Krakow (an underage youth). The succession conflicts in Hungary led to a civil war, during which two nobles, Ján Huňady, a condottiere from Hunedoara and Ján Jiskra from Moravian Brandýs nad Orlicí, began their careers. Both fought on one side against Hussites, Brothers, and the Ottomans, but also against each other, as supporters of two opposing groups and interests of their kings, later under a common king with differing ideas and attitudes about governing Upper Hungary (today's Slovakia), with strong ties to Bratislava and Vienna. Jiskra's role was to protect the interests of the Habsburg candidate for the Hungarian throne (which caused hostility in Budapest). Essentially, he was on the front line, a harbinger of the formation of the Habsburg monarchy.
Following an agreement among the nobility, Jiskra in 1445 became one of the seven Hajtmans (regional leaders) who governed the country (on Slovak territory, this included Ján Jiskra of Brandýs, Pongrác of Szentmiklós, and regional judge Imrich Bubek). However, it later became clear that this was not a good decision. Disagreements, conflicts, and armed clashes grew among the hajtman. In 1446, the Hungarian assembly appointed Ján Huňady (who mainly defended Hungarian interests) as the main governor (land administrator) Ján Huňady (Huňady, who defended mainly Hungarian interests, immediately clashed with Jiskra). But the situation did not improve much. Nobles schemed against each other, forming alliances and breaking them as needed, fighting among themselves. The population was subjected to violence and looting. The southern parts of the country were threatened by the Turks, but Huňady managed to defeat them several times. He also tried to undermine Jiskra's power in Slovakia. The fighting ended inconclusively, and enemies signed a truce. In the autumn of 1448, Huňady led a major campaign against the Ottoman Empire. The Battle of Kosovo resulted in a catastrophic defeat for the Hungarian army. Huňady barely escaped with his life. For several years afterward, he managed to maintain peace with the Turks, allowing him to focus on domestic issues. He organized multiple campaigns against Jiskra, culminating in the Battle of Lučenec in summer 1451.
Army Strength
Jiskra’s army, which excelled not only in tactics but also in equipment produced in Slovak towns, numbered around 5,000 men (Jiskra’s fighters included not only Czechs and Slovaks but also Moravians, Silesians, Austrians, Poles, and even Hungarians.). Huňady’s army, about 12,000 men strong, consisted of various types of troops, from Banderiums of the noble seats to Kumán cavalry units and a small number of mercenaries (according to some written sources, Jiskra had only 3,000 to 4,000 men, and Huňady up to 20,000)..
Battle
In mid-August 1451, Huňady occupied Lučenec, which had previously been burned by Jiskra’s troops, and began besieging the fortified Monastery of St. Stephen (a Cistercian monastery founded in the 12th century), defended by a 500-strong garrison of Jiskra’s soldiers led by the experienced commander Matej of Kněžice. The Lučenec monastery was presumably surrounded by a stone wall, and it is believed that the defenders dug a new ditch and reinforced the rampart with wooden palisades and log structures. The garrison heroically defended this fortified position, repelling several attacks. Huňady then changed tactics and decided to starve them out. He ordered an additional rampart to be built around the fortress (also against possible sorties) and thus confined the defenders to a relatively small area. This further tightened the siege, and the summer heat, hunger, and thirst were expected to finish the work.  Knowing their hopeless situation, the defenders tried to negotiate. They demanded free departure as a condition. Huňady did not allow it and set up sharpened stakes, demonstrating that he would impale them all. The only hope then was Ján Jiskra. And he did not disappoint them.
At that time, Jiskra was gathering troops in northeastern Slovakia. From there, he marched quickly to Lučenec. On September 7, Hussite wagons appeared near the town, and signal fires were lit on a nearby hill to announce his approach to the besieged. His army was hastily assembled mainly from garrisons of towns and castles under his control (evidence of their past presence is reflected in the names of some villages in Novohrad such as Praha or Czech Březovo). Unlike Huňady’s troops, these were all very well-organized, experienced mercenaries. Huňady, out of caution, blocked the roads leading to the town upon arriving at Lučenec, but Jiskra’s infantry managed to break through the barricades and clear the passages for cavalry and war chariots. Huňady seemingly underestimated his considerably weaker opponent and overestimated his influence over the noble Bandériums, although it was clear that some Hungarian nobles were jealous of his political and military successes. According to some written sources, he reportedly confidently said before the battle that his own couriers would be enough to disperse the enemy with a whip. The older Slovak historian František Sasinek and Czech writer Alois Jirásek both mention an alleged conversation between the commanding officer announcing Jiskra’s arrival and Huňady: “Well, they are heading to their misfortune. Three thousand! I have twenty thousand of them. We’ll have them for breakfast.” The commander supposedly replied: “And we won’t have enough of them even for dinner, sir!” That is the extent of literary creation. The reality was probably different.
Huňady divided his units. A smaller part under the command of Štefan Bubek (from the noble Bubekov family, also written as Bebek) was to continue besieging the monastery (Huňady left only part of the auxiliary units, guards, and the wounded at the main camp), while the other, larger part, led by the vanguard of Jäger-bishop Ladislav Hédervári, moved against Jiskra. The Hussite wagon fort engaged in combat with Jiskra’s army. Jiskra’s men, mainly thanks to their skillfully constructed wagon fort, repelled Hédervári’s units with arrow and firearm fire. The claim by several writers that the use of firearms was not yet common in Hungary at that time (the bishop’s men were reportedly quite surprised by this shooting) is refuted by numerous confirmed reports of such weapons being available in Huňady’s army as well. Jiskra’s mercenaries had an advantage in hand-to-hand combat. They proved to be better trained and experienced fighters, unlike many members of the Hungarian bands. Ultimately, the combat skills, better training, battle experience, possibly the effective use of new weapons, and determination balanced the numerical superiority of Huňady’s forces. Jiskra’s soldiers, through skillful maneuvering, pushed the most effective weapon of medieval warfare—the heavy Hungarian cavalry—into the marshy terrain near the stream Slatinka (marshlands around Lučenec are even documented on maps from the early 20th century). The heavy riders lost their maneuverability and striking power. Huňady perceived the danger and hurried to support them with additional forces. However, something he had not anticipated happened. The defenders of the monastery attacked and broke through the weakened besiegers’ forces, entering their back. Huňady’s entire army then scattered, and the commander himself fled to avoid capture. Štefan Bubek fell, and among others, the Jagiellonian bishop Ladislav was taken prisoner.
Aftermath
The fighting continued between them, and after some successes, Huňady and his forces signed a peace treaty at Rimavská Sobota at the end of 1451 (Huňady had to pay Jiskra war reparations and continue to respect his power in Slovakia), which was less favorable for Jiskra than the peace of 1450, but reflected his actual position and power. Essentially, the status quo of that time was confirmed, with the difference that the castle Plaveč was no longer part of Jiskra’s domain (its captain Aksamít defected from Jiskra), and Kežmarok (its captain Mikuláš Brcál) also defected from Jiskra, for which Jiskra was to receive compensation of 10,600 gold coins. The defection of two of Jiskra’s old comrades signaled that his position was shaken. Ján Huňady also attempted to limit Jiskra’s power diplomatically. He aimed for the towns of Levoča, Bardejov, and Košice to defect, which he succeeded in doing in 1452. Huňady’s success was also aided by the relaxed discipline in Jiskra’s army and its partial disintegration. The renewed peace treaty with Huňady in August 1452 restricted Jiskra’s domain to the towns of Levoča, Spiš Castle, and the income from tithes in Kežmarok and Stará Ľubovňa. Early in 1453, Ladislaus the Posthumous, upon ascending the throne (reaching majority), appointed J. Huňady as regional captain, and on February 6, a session in Bratislava deprived Jiskra of all property and expelled him from Hungary.

The Oldest Inscription in Jasov Cave
An inscription from 1452 in Jasov Cave, written with charcoal on a limestone wall, states that Ján Jiskra of Brandýs’s army defeated Ján Huňady at the Battle of Lučenec.
